t: A pure term insurance policy with a 20-year term pays which of the following if the life assured survives the full term?
e: A pure term plan provides only a death benefit during the term; there is no maturity or survival benefit, which is why it is the cheapest form of life cover. A return-of-premium variant would refund premiums, but a pure term plan does not.

t: Under a money-back policy with a sum assured of ₹5,00,000 and term of 20 years, survival benefits of 20% are paid at the end of the 5th, 10th and 15th years. If the life assured dies in the 17th policy year, what does the nominee receive (ignoring bonuses)?
e: In a money-back plan the full sum assured is payable on death during the term regardless of survival benefits already paid, so the nominee receives ₹5,00,000 plus accrued bonuses. Only the maturity payment is reduced by the survival benefits already paid.

t: What is the minimum lock-in period for a unit linked insurance policy under IRDAI regulations?
e: IRDAI prescribes a five-year lock-in for ULIPs from the date of commencement; surrender or partial withdrawal proceeds cannot be paid before completion of five years. The three-year lock-in applied only to policies issued before September 2010.

t: An annuity that continues to pay the annuitant for life and, after his death, pays the spouse for her lifetime is called:
o: Deferred annuity with return of purchase price
e: A joint life last survivor annuity is payable as long as either of the two annuitants is alive. An annuity certain pays for a fixed number of years irrespective of survival.

t: Under a one-year renewable group term assurance (OYRGTA) scheme, the premium is:
o: Recalculated at each annual renewal based on the group's age profile and experience
Fixed for the entire working life of the members
Determined by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation
e: OYRGTA cover is renewed yearly and the premium is re-rated at renewal using the current membership, age distribution and claims experience of the group. It is a pure risk cover with no savings element.

t: Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic elements considered by an actuary while pricing a traditional life insurance product?
e: The classical premium basis uses assumptions on mortality, interest and expenses (plus lapse and profit margin). Market share is a business objective, not a pricing element.

t: The IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024 came into force with effect from:
e: The consolidated Insurance Products Regulations, 2024 were notified in March 2024 and took effect from 1 April 2024, replacing six earlier product-related regulations including the Non-Linked and Linked products regulations of 2019.

t: Under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the maximum aggregate deduction available for life insurance premium together with other eligible investments is:
e: The overall ceiling under Section 80C (read with Section 80CCE) is ₹1,50,000 per financial year. The ₹50,000 additional deduction under Section 80CCD(1B) is only for NPS contributions.

t: A ULIP policyholder with regular annualised premium of ₹1,00,000 and age 30 must be offered a minimum sum assured on death of at least:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). IRDAI requires a minimum death benefit of 7 times the annualised premium for regular premium policies (1.25 times for single premium), so ₹7,00,000; the earlier 10-times rule was reduced in 2019.

t: A home loan borrower wants cover whose sum assured reduces each year in line with the outstanding loan. The most suitable product is:
e: Decreasing term assurance, often sold as mortgage redemption insurance, has a sum assured that falls in step with the outstanding loan balance, keeping premiums low. Level term keeps the sum assured constant.

t: Which of the following is an example of a 'living benefit' under a life insurance product?
o: Death benefit paid to the nominee
Survival benefit under a money-back plan
e: Living benefits are payable to the policyholder during his lifetime, such as survival benefits, maturity benefit, annuity instalments or critical illness lump sums. Death and funeral benefits are payable only on death.

t: Under IRDAI norms, the minimum annuity instalment that an insurer may offer under an annuity product is:
e: The minimum annuity amount is ₹1,000 per month (or its equivalent for other frequencies), a limit retained in the 2024 product framework; for NPS subscribers and certain cases lower amounts may be permitted.

t: A pure endowment assurance pays the sum assured:
o: Only on survival to the end of the term
Only on death during the term
On death or survival, whichever is earlier
Twice: once on death and again on maturity
e: A pure endowment pays only if the life assured survives the term; nothing (or at most a return of premiums) is payable on earlier death. An ordinary endowment combines a pure endowment with term assurance.

t: Under the Insurance Act, 1938, the maximum share of surplus from a participating fund that may be allocated to shareholders is:
e: Section 49 of the Insurance Act limits the shareholders' share of surplus in the participating business to 10%, so at least 90% of distributable surplus goes to with-profits policyholders as bonus.

t: The mortality table currently used as the reference table by Indian life insurers for pricing and valuation is:
e: The Institute of Actuaries of India published the IALM 2012-14 table based on Indian insured lives experience, and it is the standard reference table; the earlier LIC 94-96 and IALM 06-08 tables have been superseded.

t: The maximum assurance benefit under the statutory Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI) scheme, as revised in 2021, is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). EDLI benefit was enhanced to a maximum of ₹7 lakh (minimum ₹2.5 lakh) for death in service; employers may substitute it with a group term policy offering at least equal benefits.

t: The free-look period available to a life insurance policyholder from the date of receipt of the policy document, as per the 2024 regulatory framework, is:
o: 15 days for offline and 30 days for electronic policies
e: The IRDAI 2024 framework extended the free-look period to 30 days from receipt of the policy document for all policies, replacing the earlier 15-day period (30 days only for distance-marketed policies).

t: Which group life product is commonly used by employers as a substitute for the statutory Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI) scheme?
o: Group term life assurance in lieu of EDLI
e: EPFO permits employers to opt out of EDLI if they provide a group term insurance giving benefits not less favourable than EDLI, which insurers offer as a group term policy in lieu of EDLI.

t: A limited payment whole life policy differs from an ordinary whole life policy in that:
o: Sum assured is payable only on maturity at age 100
Premiums are payable only for a specified number of years while cover continues for life
It does not participate in bonuses
e: In a limited payment whole life policy premiums stop after a fixed term (say 20 years or age 60), but the life cover continues till death. Ordinary whole life requires premiums throughout life.

t: The maximum fund management charge (FMC) that an insurer may levy on a ULIP fund under IRDAI norms is:
e: IRDAI caps the fund management charge at 1.35% p.a. of the fund value; the discontinued policy fund has a lower cap of 0.50% p.a.

t: Under a deferred annuity plan, the period between the date of purchase and the date the first annuity instalment becomes payable is known as the:
e: During the deferment period the purchase price accumulates; at the vesting date the annuity starts. The vesting date marks the end of deferment, not the whole period.

t: A life assured holding a term plan of ₹50 lakh with an accidental death benefit rider of ₹25 lakh dies in a road accident. The nominee receives:
e: Accidental death benefit is payable in addition to the base sum assured when death is caused by an accident, so ₹50 lakh base plus ₹25 lakh rider = ₹75 lakh.

t: A level premium under a whole life policy is higher than the actual cost of risk in the early years. The excess is:
o: Returned to the policyholder as a bonus
Paid as commission to the agent
Accumulated as a reserve to meet the higher cost of risk in later years
e: Because mortality rises with age, a level premium overcharges in early years and undercharges later; the early excess builds the policy reserve that funds the later shortfall and forms the basis of surrender value.

t: A life insurance policy (other than ULIP) issued on 1 June 2023 has an annual premium of ₹6 lakh. Under Section 10(10D), the maturity proceeds will be:
o: Fully exempt because premium is less than sum assured
Taxable only if the policy is surrendered
Exempt up to ₹5 lakh and taxable beyond
Taxable, since aggregate premium exceeds ₹5 lakh for policies issued on or after 1 April 2023
e: Finance Act 2023 withdrew the 10(10D) exemption for non-ULIP policies issued on or after 1 April 2023 where aggregate annual premium exceeds ₹5 lakh; death benefit remains exempt.

t: A double endowment policy pays:
o: Sum assured on death and double the sum assured on survival to maturity
Double the sum assured on death and sum assured on maturity
Sum assured on both death and maturity
Double the sum assured on accidental death only
e: In a double endowment the survival benefit at maturity is twice the sum assured payable on death, which makes it attractive for lives with slightly impaired health who expect to survive.

t: Which classification correctly pairs a product with its primary purpose?
o: Immediate annuity – protection against premature death
e: Endowment plans combine death cover with a savings element payable on maturity. Term is pure protection, annuities address longevity risk, and ULIP returns are market-linked, not guaranteed.

t: A non-participating (non-par) savings product is characterised by:
o: Bonuses declared annually based on surplus
Returns linked to the NAV of a fund
Benefits that are fully guaranteed at the outset and no share in profits
Premiums that vary every year with investment performance
e: Non-par products offer pre-defined guaranteed benefits (e.g., guaranteed additions or income) and the policyholder does not participate in the insurer's surplus; the investment risk is borne by the insurer.

t: A non-ULIP policy issued in 2015 has a sum assured of ₹5,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹60,000. On maturity, the proceeds will be:
o: Taxable, because the premium exceeds 10% of the sum assured
Exempt because premium is below ₹5 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). For policies issued on or after 1 April 2012, Section 10(10D) exemption is lost if premium in any year exceeds 10% of the actual capital sum assured; here ₹60,000 is 12% of ₹5 lakh. Death benefits remain exempt.

t: If a ULIP with an annualised premium of ₹40,000 is discontinued in the first policy year, the maximum discontinuance charge the insurer may levy is:
o: Nil, since discontinuance charges are prohibited
Lower of 6% of annualised premium or fund value, subject to a maximum of ₹6,000
20% of fund value without any cap
Lower of 20% of annualised premium or fund value, subject to a maximum of ₹3,000
e: For annualised premium up to ₹50,000, the first-year discontinuance charge is the lower of 20% of AP or FV, capped at ₹3,000. The 6%/₹6,000 limit applies when AP exceeds ₹50,000. No charge applies from the fifth year onwards.

t: Under IRDAI norms for pension products, on vesting the policyholder may commute up to what proportion of the accumulated corpus as a lump sum?
e: IRDAI permits commutation of up to 60% of the vesting benefit, with the balance (at least 40%) to be used to purchase an annuity, aligned with the NPS structure. The earlier limit was one-third.

t: A critical illness rider under a life policy typically pays:
o: A lump sum on first diagnosis of a listed critical illness, after the survival period
Daily cash for each day of hospitalisation
The sum assured only on death due to the illness
e: CI riders are benefit-based: a pre-defined lump sum is paid on diagnosis of a covered condition (cancer, heart attack, stroke, etc.), usually after a survival period of 30 days and a waiting period of 90 days from commencement.

t: A group credit life scheme sold with personal loans generally provides:
o: A level sum assured equal to the original loan for the full term
An endowment benefit to the borrower on repayment of the loan
A decreasing cover equal to the outstanding loan payable to the lender on the borrower's death
Cover only for the lender's own employees
e: Credit life cover protects the lender and the borrower's family by paying the outstanding loan balance on death; the cover reduces in line with the amortisation schedule.

t: Under the 'Use and File' procedure introduced by IRDAI, a life insurer may:
o: Launch only group products without IRDAI approval
Launch any product only after prior written approval of IRDAI
Launch products without any filing to IRDAI at all
Launch an approved category of product after internal approval by its Product Management Committee and file with IRDAI subsequently
e: Use and File allows insurers to launch products after approval by the Product Management Committee and Board-approved product management policy, filing the details with IRDAI within the prescribed period, speeding time-to-market compared with File and Use.

t: Non-disclosure of a material fact by the proposer makes the contract:
o: Voidable at the option of the insurer
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Breach of utmost good faith renders the contract voidable, not void; the insurer may elect to avoid it (subject to Section 45 for life).

t: Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938 (as amended in 2015), a life insurance policy cannot be called in question on any ground after:
o: 3 years from the date of issue, revival or rider addition, whichever is later
2 years from the date of issue
1 year from the date of issue
5 years from the date of issue
e: The 2015 amendment made policies incontestable on any ground, including fraud, after three years from the date of policy, commencement of risk, revival or rider addition, whichever is later.

t: A return-of-premium term plan (TROP) with annual premium ₹12,000 and term 30 years is held to maturity. Ignoring GST, the maturity benefit is:
e: TROP refunds the total base premiums paid (₹12,000 × 30 = ₹3,60,000) on survival to maturity; it carries no bonus because it is a non-participating product, and GST and rider premiums are excluded from the refund.

t: The feature of a money-back policy that makes its premium higher than an endowment policy of the same sum assured and term is:
o: Periodic survival benefits paid during the term while full death cover continues
e: Because the insurer pays out part of the sum assured periodically yet continues to carry the full death risk, the money-back plan requires higher premiums than a plain endowment.

t: Which charge in a ULIP is deducted from the premium before units are allocated?
e: The premium allocation charge is a percentage of premium deducted upfront, with only the balance invested in units. Mortality and policy administration charges are recovered by cancelling units, and FMC is adjusted in the NAV.

t: An 'annuity with return of purchase price' is attractive to annuitants mainly because:
o: The purchase price is refunded to the nominee on the annuitant's death, leaving an estate
It gives the highest annuity rate
It can be surrendered at any time without penalty
e: Return of purchase price ensures the capital is not lost on early death, but the annuity rate is lower than a pure life annuity because the insurer must return the corpus.

t: Under IRDAI product norms, the premium for a non-health rider (such as accidental death benefit) attached to a non-linked policy should not exceed:
e: Non-health riders are limited to 30% of the base policy premium each, while health riders may go up to 100% of the base premium; rider benefits (other than health) are also capped at the base sum assured.

t: A group superannuation scheme managed by a life insurer is primarily intended to provide:
o: Gratuity payments as per the Payment of Gratuity Act
Retirement pension to employees through accumulation of contributions
e: Superannuation schemes accumulate employer (and sometimes employee) contributions to provide a pension at retirement; the insurer manages the fund and typically offers annuities at retirement.

t: The 'risk premium' for a one-year term cover of ₹10,00,000 on a life whose probability of death in the year is 0.002 is:
e: Risk (natural) premium = probability of death × sum assured = 0.002 × ₹10,00,000 = ₹2,000, before loading for expenses, interest and profit.

t: Which of the following statements about Section 10(10D) exemption for ULIPs is correct?
o: ULIPs issued on or after 1 February 2021 with aggregate annual premium above ₹2.5 lakh lose the exemption on maturity proceeds
All ULIP maturity proceeds are exempt irrespective of premium
ULIP death benefits are taxable if premium exceeds ₹2.5 lakh
Only ULIPs with a term below 10 years are exempt
e: Finance Act 2021 made maturity/surrender proceeds of high-premium ULIPs (aggregate premium > ₹2.5 lakh p.a., issued on or after 1-2-2021) taxable as capital gains; death benefits stay exempt.

t: A standard individual term product named 'Saral Jeevan Bima' was mandated by IRDAI with a sum assured range of:
e: Saral Jeevan Bima is a standardised pure term plan with sum assured of ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh (in multiples of ₹50,000), entry age 18–65 and policy term 5–40 years, with a 45-day waiting period for non-accidental death.

t: A terminal bonus under a participating policy is:
o: Guaranteed and declared at policy inception
A one-time bonus paid at the time of exit (death or maturity), reflecting the policy's share of accumulated surplus
Deducted from the sum assured on surrender
e: Terminal (final) bonus is non-guaranteed and paid only once, on maturity or death, for policies that have run for a minimum period; it is not added yearly like a reversionary bonus.

t: Deduction for life insurance premium under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act is available up to an overall limit of:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹1,50,000 aggregate for all 80C items; premium qualifies only up to 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012.

t: Which statement about a convertible term assurance policy is INCORRECT?
o: It can be converted into an endowment or whole life policy within a specified period
Conversion is allowed without fresh evidence of health
On conversion the premium changes to that of the new plan
The option to convert can be exercised at any time till maturity of the term plan
e: The conversion option must be exercised within a specified window (often before the last two years of the term), not at any time up to maturity. The other statements correctly describe convertible term plans.

t: A policyholder of a ULIP wants to move accumulated units from an equity fund to a debt fund without changing where future premiums are invested. The option to use is:
e: A switch transfers existing units between funds; premium redirection changes the allocation of future premiums. Most insurers allow a few free switches per year.

t: Under the National Pension System, on exit at age 60 a subscriber must use at least what percentage of the corpus to buy an annuity from an empanelled life insurer?
e: NPS rules require at least 40% of the accumulated corpus to be annuitised at normal exit; up to 60% may be withdrawn as a tax-free lump sum.

t: Where a life insurance claim requires no investigation, the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) framework of 2024 requires the insurer to settle the death claim within how many days of receiving all documents?
e: The 2024 regulations tightened timelines: 15 days for claims not needing investigation and 45 days where investigation is warranted; delay attracts penal interest at bank rate plus 2%.
